examples.question_text: Find the global maximum and global minimum values of $f(x)=x^{3}-6x^{2}+7$ on $-1\le x\le 6$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^{2}-12x\\f''(x)&=6x-12\\3x(x-4)&=0\\x&=0\\x&=4\end{aligned}$
Both stationary points lie in the domain. Since $f''(0)=-12<0$, there is a local maximum at $x=0$. Since $f''(4)=12>0$, there is a local minimum at $x=4$.
Compare the stationary values and endpoints:
$\begin{aligned}f(-1)&=-1-6+7=0\\f(0)&=7\\f(4)&=64-96+7=-25\\f(6)&=216-216+7=7\end{aligned}$
The global maximum is $7$, attained at both $x=0$ and $x=6$. The global minimum is $-25$, attained at $x=4$.

examples.question_text: Find the global maximum and global minimum values of $f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+4$ on $7\le x\le 9$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=3x^{2}-18x\\3x(x-6)&=0\\x&=0\\x&=6\end{aligned}$
Neither stationary point lies in $7\le x\le9$, so discard both. The function is continuous and differentiable throughout this interval; compare its endpoints:
$\begin{aligned}f(7)&=343-441+4=-94\\f(9)&=729-729+4=4\end{aligned}$
The global maximum is $4$, at $x=9$. The global minimum is $-94$, at $x=7$.

examples.question_text: Find the global maximum and global minimum values of $f(x)=x+\dfrac{16}{x}$ on $1\le x\le8$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}f'(x)&=1-\frac{16}{x^{2}}\\1-\frac{16}{x^{2}}&=0\\x^{2}&=16\\x&=\pm4\end{aligned}$
Only $x=4$ lies in the domain. Here $f''(x)=\dfrac{32}{x^{3}}>0$, so the stationary point is a local minimum.
Compare its value with both endpoints:
$\begin{aligned}f(1)&=1+16=17\\f(4)&=4+4=8\\f(8)&=8+2=10\end{aligned}$
The global maximum is $17$, at $x=1$. The global minimum is $8$, at $x=4$.

examples.question_text: Explain why $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-1}$ has neither a global maximum nor a global minimum on $-2\le x\le4$, $x\ne1$.
examples.solution_text:
$f'(x)=-\dfrac{1}{(x-1)^{2}}$ is never zero. The function is undefined at the excluded point $x=1$.
As $x\to1^{-}$, the denominator approaches zero through negative values, so $f(x)\to-\infty$.
As $x\to1^{+}$, the denominator approaches zero through positive values, so $f(x)\to+\infty$.
The function is unbounded below and above. Neither endpoint can supply a smallest or largest value, and infinite limits are not attained function values. There is no global minimum and no global maximum.

examples.derivation: Differentiating gives f'(x)=3x(x-4), with stationary points 0 and 4. The second derivative gives a local maximum at 0 and local minimum at 4. Candidate values at -1, 0, 4 and 6 are respectively 0, 7, -25 and 7. Thus the global maximum is 7 at both 0 and 6, and the global minimum is -25 at 4.
Differentiating gives f'(x)=3x(x-6). Both stationary points lie outside [7,9]. Endpoint values are f(7)=-94 and f(9)=4; these are the global minimum and maximum respectively.

Differentiating gives f'(x)=1-16/x², whose zeros are ±4. Only 4 is admissible, and f''(x)=32/x³ is positive throughout the domain. Candidate values f(1)=17, f(4)=8 and f(8)=10 establish the maximum 17 and minimum 8.

The plotted function 8+3x²-x³ increases from (0,8) to (2,12), then decreases to (4,-8). Its derivative is 3x(2-x), confirming these heights and locations. Both extrema fit within the authored axis ranges and match the solution annotations. The student-facing solution correctly reads the graph.

Differentiating gives -1/(x-1)², with no stationary points. Approaching 1 from below gives an unbounded negative limit; approaching from above gives an unbounded positive limit. Consequently neither a largest nor a smallest attained value exists.
